newsitem.title: GERMANY: Coffee price rises seen hitting German retail sale.
newsitem.headline: Coffee price rises seen hitting German retail sale.

text.p: Planned price rises in Germany's roasted coffee market may hurt retail sales after an initial period of consumer hoarding, roaster J.J. Darboven said on Tuesday.
Darboven GmbH's marketing head, Horst Hentz, told a news conference he envisaged a negative consumer reaction if prices remained above 10 marks per 0.5 kilos for long periods.
"Ten marks is the pain threshold, but we would go above that price if we needed to pay that much to maintain our quality blends," he said.
German roasters will add 1.50 marks per 0.5 kg to ex-plant prices as of March 10 in a bid to offset rising costs.
Prices of arabicas have risen by 50 percent over the last two months, and the dollar advanced to 1.68 marks from 1.45 in that period.
Hentz said a second round of retail price rises could become necessary.
Arabicas have been rallying because of the possibility of strike action by some Brazilian port workers and on news supporting a tightening 1997/98 supply scenario.
The average German retail price had dropped to 7.01 marks in January 1997 from 7.98 a year earlier, Hentz said.
Darboven's "Idee Kaffee" flagship product cost 7.17 marks, but its Moevenpick Gourmet coffee was poised to go above 10 marks in the first round of price increases.
Hentz said Darboven sales volumes in January/February were 40.2 percent above those in the same 1996 period.
This reflected hoarding by retail chains in response to anticipated consumer hoarding in the run-up to Easter holidays at the end of March, a seasonal peak for coffee consumption.
"Consumers won't feel the effect of price rises in March as supermarkets will offer price discounts to attract customers, but consumption could fall strongly after Easter," he said.
